column16: This webinar explores how drawing on learners’ own languages (pedagogical translanguaging) can enhance inclusion, foster collaboration, and strengthen communication skills.
column17: Students bring rich linguistic backgrounds into the classroom, yet their first languages are often overlooked in English learning. This session makes the case that embracing linguistic diversity helps students engage more deeply, build confidence, develop stronger plurilingual skills, and take pride in their linguistic identities. Even when teachers don’t share their students’ languages or work in classrooms with multiple first languages, they can still apply practical strategies to create a more supportive and effective learning environment.
column18: I learn the importance of an inclusive learning environment where students feel valued when teacher acknowledges their first languages. This helps to foster students' language acquisition. Therefore I aim to include some fun activities in class that incorporate students' first languages skills.
column19: Play some fun games in class (can use chatgpt to generate) which involve students to make correlations from their own languages such as finding words that are the same in my language and English within a time limit (e.g. pizza, taco) or co-constructions where students reconstruct a text in their language to English. Other activities include "learn my language" - learners think of mistakes that English speakers make when learning their language and "same story different languages" - students compare news stories that are written in their own languages and discuss similarities/differences with the English versions.

column16: This webinar will focus on the importance of academic vocabulary to English learners preparing to study at university, providing techniques and resources to support the development and assessment of knowledge and the use of academic lexis.
column17: The webinar discussed the importance of academic vocabulary to English learners preparing to study at university. I have learnt that it is very important to teach students words on the high frequency list first, focusing on form, meaning and use of those words. According to Prof. Coxhead, students need about 5000 - 9000 word families to reach 98% coverage of written academic texts and 4000 word families for 95% coverage of spoken academic texts. She also introduces the TFA framework which can be used to assess the effectiveness of an activity/task to build students' academic vocabulary.
column18: This webinar is very useful for my teaching as I usually have to think of activities to build my students' vocabulary in the EAP courses. I will use the TFA approach introduced by Prof. Coxhead in evaluating the level of efficiency of the activities I design for my students. Also, it is crucial to know that students need to be familiarised with more academic word families than we often cover in class in order to comprehend written and spoken academic texts. This will help them to perform better in university courses.

column16: The availability of GenAI applications (such as ChatGPT) and students’ easy access to them means that we can’t continue as if they didn’t exist. In student assessment what should remain the same and what needs to change? The webinar will focus on the principles we need to inform our assessment practices and their implications.
column17: GenAI is here to stay and is evolving; hence, education and assessment face a big challenge. We need to change our assessment practice to avoid students' cheating and ensure learning happens. The speaker then went on to explain 3 key roles of assessment and discuss some suggestions to ensure students meet the learning outcomes according to the set standards.
column18: The webinar suggests some very useful strategies which I can apply in designing tasks and the way I carry out assessments at my colleges to avoid students' AI use. For example, continue to give students feedback to benefit themselves and grade students' success always by meeting standards, never by marks. Besides, do random oral checks for assurance that students did not use AI in their writings. Identify conditions in which it is legitimate for students to use/not use genAI in assessment. Prioritise validity over cheating. Build students evaluative judgement to use AI tools effectively (ie. develop prompting/judging skills, and the importance of checking and iteration). Importantly, have more specific, unique, current and contextualised tasks.
column19: Provide students with more feedback along the way, let them know "what good look like". Make sure students meet learning outcomes through formative assessment, not just summative assessment. Design tasks that separate students from using AI in test rooms and are more personalised to avoid AI use. Have random checks orally to confirm if students wrote the task themselves. Demonstrate when is acceptable to use AI.

column17: Join Associate Professor Kellie Toohey for an inspiring webinar, where she shares her highly successful insights and authentic voice on online teaching. Dr. Toohey’s approach has garnered outstanding student feedback, and she experiences no drop-off in her online classes—reflecting her remarkable ability to keep students engaged and enthusiastic. Her methods go beyond the technicalities of digital tools; they are rooted in a human-centred pedagogical approach that prioritises connection and trust.  Dr. Toohey will walk us through her strategies for fostering a safe, inclusive online environment where students feel encouraged to participate and express themselves. She’ll delve into the “magic” behind her approach, which includes normalising the online learning experience, embracing pauses in conversation, and making every student feel heard and valued. Through her dedication to building genuine interactions and comfort in her virtual classrooms, Dr. Toohey brings humanity into online teaching, creating a space where students thrive. This session promises actionable takeaways for enhancing online learning environments, making it essential for educators looking to deepen their digital teaching impact.

column16: Give effective instructions for learning activities. Monitor progress during a learning activity. Reflect on learning after an activity.
column17: I learn from this webinar to plan my activity according to three stages, as the beginning and the end are equally important as the middle. Often in class I find myself guilty of rushing to the activity and then having to explain again and again to students, which I will aim to fix. Besides, using ICQs instead of asking "do you understand?" and taking notes while students are doing the activity are great tips, too.
column18: I will use it to plan every activity in my class more thoroughly, making sure all activities have three parts: the beginning, the middle and the end. Then, focus on giving instructions clearly using simple language and gestures. Next make sure students understand the task by asking ICQs. During the activity, take notes of students' language, give praises and provide feedbacks. It is important to sit near the participants, not standing over. In the end, reflect and correct any mistakes I've noted down and then transition to the next activity.
column19: Plan each activity carefully, use gestures, speak slowly, demonstrate and ask ICQs to make sure students understand the task. Then take notes during the activity and finally give feedbacks/ reflect in the end.

column9: Read the article "Course planning" written by Joanna Dossetor
column16: The goal of this article is to enhance a teacher’s ability to plan courses and lessons effectively. This involves developing skills in both long-term and short-term planning, being able to see the bigger picture of a course (e.g., a 100-hour course) while also focusing on the finer details of individual lessons and activities (e.g., a 15-minute activity). Additionally, the goal is to build confidence in teaching by helping teachers plan in a coherent and organised manner, leading to more focused and productive classroom time.
column17: I learn from this article the importance of both long-term and short-term planning for effective teaching. A balanced routine with variety keeps students engaged. Planning with coherence and organisation builds confidence, enhances efficiency, and allows for a structured, engaging learning experience that motivates students and fosters continuous progress.
column18: I can apply this by creating a clear course structure that balances long-term goals with detailed lesson planning. Besides, incorporate familiar routines for continuity while adding variety to maintain student engagement. I will plan with flexibility and reflection, ensuring my lessons are well-organised, purposeful, and tailored to my students' needs.
column19: I will start by outlining a clear course structure, focusing on long-term goals while planning individual lessons with attention to detail. I’ll incorporate routine activities, also known as 'threads', for consistency and experiment with varying teaching methods to maintain engagement. Additionally, I’ll create a personalised “recipe book” for effective, engaging lesson activities.

column16: Learning how to utilise AI more in the classroom, in particular with Cambridge materials.
column17: Conversational AI responds to spoken or text inputs - students can practice by themselves and make sure their pronunciation is good enough for the AI to understand.  Use AI to come with questions on topics related to the text book for ss to discuss.  Teach ss language to ask AI questions.  Use Google + Bard to practice listening by asking it questions, e.g.'Tell me 6 encouraging facts about the future of the environment'.  The text appears, but the you can also listen to the answer.  Text created AI is better for levels over B1, because ss it is more challenging ,especially when give the opportunity to listen to what is being presented. Let students use GenAI tools to develop their critical thinking and digital literacy. One example of this for secondary or adult learners is to give them a debate topic, and ask them to collect different arguments or opinions from their classmates, a GenAI chatbot, and other resources on the internet. Ask them to compare and evaluate the information they have collected. This activity will help your students understand how to use GenAI tools responsibly alongside other sources of information, and the benefits and drawbacks of GenAI tools.  Chatbots can produce factually incorrect information, known as a ‘hallucination’ (Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year 2023.) They also don’t always do what you want. Carefully check any output to make sure it is accurate and appropriate. After using AI, have students write some reflections on how beneficial they felt the activity was.

column16: Keeping up to date with the changes in computer based Cambridge testing
column17: Cambridge English Qualifications Digital test the same knowledge and skills as paper-based exams, but through a digital exam experience. Taken on a computer, these exams give students control over elements of the listening, writing and reading, helping them to do their best in their own way. Each candidate receives a randomised set of questions, all equal in terms of task types and difficulty. This means that everyone can focus fully on their own exam and the risk of any answers being copied is minimised.  Results will only take between 5-10 days instead of up to 6 weeks.  Reading (and Use of English), listening and writing are basically the same as the paper-based test.  The speaking test remains face-to-face 'to help develop real word communication skills'.  The new digital tests are available from March 2024, not sure where though.  Testing may be available 365 days a year, depending on centre.

column16: In this webinar, ELICOS teachers from English Australia member colleges present practical examples of teaching in a Hybrid setting. column19: I will apply these ideas in my teaching methods by planning carefully CCQs and tasks to help students acquire the meanings of vocabulary more easily. Don't go overboard or use complicated words. Importantly, ask "What questions do you have? instead of "Do you have any questions?". Ask CCQs and draw timelines to visualise the actions with respect to when they happen and other aspects (what/why/how) to make sure students fully understand how to use the structure. column17: assisted with crystallisation of personal teaching methodologies through reflection and critique of content presented; and completion of reflective activities post-viewing : (see below)   For pair work activities, guiding the physical location and orientation of students (seating arrangements; choice of suitable pairs) can be extremely effective in setting up an activity by in a Heideggerian sense "throwing" students into the activity.  Keeping teacher talk to the absolute minimum means avoiding the redundant or obvious: this is valid in any communication; but even more so when interacting with non-native speakers.  I would question whether the activity is a simulation of 'real-world' situations and posit that the activity itself is the reality, challenging students to grapple with completing tasks in an English-only environment by learning to adapt- the teacher must guide this adaptation drawing on group dynamics to carry any stragglers along.  Monitoring at a distance can be more effective than sitting near student with a notepad as this can create an artificial atmosphere; or sense of simulation.  Key to ending an activity is 'differentiated learning' (i.e. increasing the level of difficulty for those that are more adept): adapt the activity in a way that means everyone finishes at the same time.  Feedback on pronunciation can sometime be more valuable than grammar, which can in some cases be treated as a separate abstracted class of learning.

Extinction: Ignore a minor distraction, such as attention-seeking misbehaviour. 2. Mild resists: non-verbal intervention strategies (eye contact, facial expression, gestures) 3. Reprimands (verbally): remind students of what they have done and show them that the teacher do not tolerate misbehaviour.
column18: -Set clear and consistent expectations for behaviour in the classroom. Ensure that students understand the rules and consequences. -Foster positive relationships with your students. Consider factors such as language proficiency, cultural differences, or specific learning needs.

column9: Scaffolding critical thinking: A process approach to teaching writing
column16: Teaching writing with efficiency and effective results.
column17: The webinar emphasised the significance of critical thinking in writing. It included the Critical Response Body Paragraph Flowchart, a tool that gives students a clear structure for structuring their ideas and developing a cohesive argument, as a practical tool for teaching and testing these skills. It walks children through making a claim, gathering evidence, assessing it, and developing a conclusion. Students will write more logical and ordered arguments if they drill the structure rigorously. A well-structured paragraph will aid in the straightforward communication of ideas, making it easier for readers to understand the assertion. With a thorough understanding of the framework, students may write more efficiently, decreasing the time spent structuring and reviewing their work. Teachers can help students develop critical thinking and improve students writing abilities.
column18: I will start by introducing this flowchart in my classes. This tool can help students visualise and understand the structure of a well-constructed paragraph. I will use it as a guide while teaching and encourage students to use it while writing; then, drill the structure: Make it a point to practice the structure outlined in the flowchart regularly. Consistent practice will help students internalise and apply the structure effectively in their writing. This could be done through regular writing assignments, workshops, and even peer review sessions; Finally, design assignments and class activities with questions that require critical thinking. Encourage students to evaluate the quality of evidence, identify biases, and develop reasoned arguments. This could involve analysing articles, debating topics, or discussing ethical dilemmas.
column19: 1. Apply a Scaffolding Approach: Gradually increase the complexity of tasks, allowing students to build their skills over time. Start with simpler tasks, provide plenty of support, and then gradually remove this support as students become more confident and skilled. 2. Model Critical Thinking: Show students how to think critically by doing so yourself. For example, I will model the process of analysing a text, identifying biases, and questioning evidence. 3. Provide Feedback: Regular and constructive feedback is essential for students to improve their critical thinking and writing skills. Make sure my feedback focuses on how well they have used the structure and applied their critical thinking skills, not just on students’ language accuracy.

column9: Assessment Symposium 2022: Assessment Practice in a Changing World
column16: The symposium helped me develop my knowledge of assessment and reporting in ELT. It helped me update my knowledge of the research and developments surrounding integrated assessment, which allows me to modernize the way I assess my learners.
column17: Through the six presentations, three keynote speakers, and two-hour live online event, I was able to gather insight into the following: 1) There is great benefit to collaboration among different institutions or centers of English as we seek to develop more quality assessment tools; 2) It may be good to look at assessment from a person-centered standpoint, giving focus on how learners have gained skills to allow them to operate well in different aspects of their lives; 3) While attempting to assess multi-literacies, it is important that we think of our learners' individual contexts; 4) Assessment research is important so we can create guidelines for effective tasks that may ease the work of ELT professionals. 5) We need to be highly flexible, especially with the new challenges we face under the new normal; 6) Creating a structure for learning progressions, perhaps in the form of a document, may be useful as a way to ensure we are assessing the right things at different points of a student's learning journey; 7) Integrated assessment, despite some perils, creates a lot of opportunities for authentic learning; 8) Interactional competence is an often neglected aspect of language learning, and it may be best for us to try and integrate it into our assessments; 9) It is important that we look into the benefits and perils of different innovations in ELT assessment so we can tailor the use of new tools to our contexts; 10) As ELT professionals, we need to do our best to communicate to larger institutions our standpoints/views if we want to see change in the system.
column18: In my own teaching, I hope to develop more formative assessment that is integrated in nature. I also want to develop scoring systems for my class that involve looking at the integration of different domains. As I hope to venture into university teaching, I would also like to use what was brought up about the ways we can make language learning as authentic and meaningful as possible for students with varied goals at university.

column9: LBB Forum 2021: Supporting learning in a changing and challenging world
column16: My personal goal in attending this forum was to learn more about how to assist in better student well-being, promoting resilence in my students and learning more about the homework clubs that 'Learning Beyond the Bell' support.
column17: During the forum I attended the introduction hour where the keynote speaker, Jacqui Francis spoke about student well-being and resilience, which helped to give context to students' behaviour in the classroom. In the 2nd hour, I attended 'Working with a growth mindset in education programs' where there was a big focus on the comparisons between 'fixed-mindset' and 'growth-mindset'. During the 3rd hour, I attended the discussion on 'Trauma informed practice to support students from a refugee background', given by Foundation House. This was where I learnt more about sensitive practices when teaching a student who has had experience with trauma or violence. Finally, in the last part of the forum, the closing address was from Saanjana Kapoor, member of CMY’s Youth Advisory Group, who shared her experiences within the education system as a tutor and student.
column18: In my future classes and tutoring sessions, I hope to take on a more growth-mindset with my students as well as using a strengths-based approach to my teaching. I will also consider how sensitive the backgrounds of my students are, when asking questions and learning more about them. As well as understanding more about the reasons for specific behaviour that they show in the classroom.

column9: Life competencies: A three-dimensional framework for this century (and beyond)
column16: Life competencies can be integrated into any subject, but they are particularly suitable for teaching English. Learning an additional language already involves many of the identified competencies such as communication, collaboration, and critical thinking. This means there is lots of scope to develop these skills further, in an integrated way, through the teaching of English. This webinar will look at how Cambridge approaches these life competencies across the learning journey.  Specifically, we will focus on what the Cambridge Language and Pedagogy Research Team have identified as life competencies and their relation to traditional models of 21st-century skills and foundational aspects of language learning. We will also explore how the understanding of the competencies translates into learning outcomes and highlight practical activities that teachers can easily integrate into secondary and adult level language lessons.
column17: I can use the 3-D Framework that Cambridge Press has developed in order to teach the 6 life competencies and the 3 foundation layers along with the target language of my language course. The PD has encouraged me and made me think more creatively when it comes to generating my own target language for my lessons.
column18: I can use the 6 life competencies as a foundation for my language teaching aims and goals and adjust them easily to the needs of the students. I will also have to make it clear to my students from the beginning of the lesson that the goal of the class is to teach a specific competency.

column16: Learn about CELT-P and CELT-S.
column17: CELT-P (Certificate in English Language Teaching – Primary) It’s a practical English teaching qualification that gives teachers the relevant skills to get the best from 6–12 year-old learners.  CELT-S (Certificate in English Language Teaching – Secondary)  It’s a practical English teaching qualification that gives teachers the relevant skills to get the best from 11–18 year old learners.  Both courses help teachers to create strategies for the key challenges of teaching English as a foreign language (TEFL) in a primary and a secondary school context, such as developing learners’ listening and speaking abilities, classroom management with large classes and motivating learners.  Teachers build on their teaching knowledge and skills, through a combination of online study and observed teaching practice with an approved trainer.

column9: LEARNING AND MEMORY: UNDERSTANDINGS FROM EDUCATIONAL NEUROSCIENCE
column16: Understand what classroom activities are helpful for different types of memory processes to aid acquisition
column17: The brain has several parts which affect memory and the information processing must go through a variety of stages. The ability to acquire information in the short term memory requires a variety of sensory stimulus, auditory and visual are particularly helpful. Then, to cement information in our long term memory we must have a semantic stimulus. To practice getting stored memories from the long term memory into the working memory (our 'memory in use') we need to practice retrieval strategies. Some rote learning methods can be helpful but they should be included alongside opportunities to learn new information (such as social activities for increased output) and form semantic associations.
column18: Lessons need to start and finish with retrieval practice -this can be achieved by reviewing what was done previously; recycling of vocabulary needs to be done continuously throughout courses  to enable students to make strong semantic associations; opportunities to learn new information need to be present in each lesson; assessment preparation should include student involvement to enhance their memorization skills.

Understanding Writing Assessment: What Every Teacher Should Know
column16: This PD by Cambridge English addresses how students' writings are to be assessed. The presenters break this down to the questions of what to assess and how to assess writing. The latter involves knowledge of how to elicit and evaluate writing. Additionally, an understanding of the underlying skills that the writing assessment covers is integral to successful teaching.  Examples include originality, coherence, structuring, etc.   Under the category of who is being assessed come issues like the learner's age, level of education, whether English is their first language, their gender, culture, level of competency, profession, and even computer literacy. Some skills are more suitable for certain levels of competency: register, for instance, would not make the marking rubric of a beginner-level student; it could, on the other hand, be a concern for students of Business English.    The whole point of writing is to produce a message. This requires learners to think about what they want to say (the cognitive aspect of writing), i.e. the message. The subskills encompassed by the cognitive include ability to plan and organise writing. Learners must have the lexicon, which includes vocabulary and grammar, to express their thoughts (the linguistic aspect of writing). Finally, learners need to understand what they are writing, why they are writing, and for whom they are writing (the socio-linguistic aspect of writing).
column17: In reality, assessing writing ability covers a range of sub-skills. Which of these subskills are being assessed would depend primarily on the level of the learner. For instance, spelling skills and handwriting are part of what would be evaluated when it comes to starter-level learners; the ability to fill in application forms or use different registers would again require a higher level of competency.   The question of why test-takers are being assessed is key to understanding how they are to be assessed. Assessing the process of the writing, which involves learners planning, reviewing, editing, and collaborating, is better suited to the classroom than in large scale test scenarios.   Finally, assessing writing responses depend on the level of learners' English language proficiency. Some writing tasks, such as those conducted at the beginner level, tend to be straight-forward. Students need to produce short answers in the right tense.  Higher-level tasks, such as extended writing, require students to understand how to use topic sentences, have paragraphs encompassing their ideas, using connectors, etc.  Variances that may emerge with teachers marking writing assessments can be dealt with through moderation meetings. This is where the rubrics can be discussed in order to produce scores that are comparable.
column18: Writing is probably one of the least practised skill in the ELICOS classroom because it is time-consuming. In my experience, few students have actively embraced the writing exercise when assigned because they often want more speaking practice and more grammar worksheets. Learners tend to ascribe their focus on these dimensions of English learning and their subsequent indifference to writing to the fact that their command over the English language becomes most apparent to them in their day-to-day life in English-speaking Australia.
column19: I intend to counter the lethargy surrounding writing by adjusting writing tasks so that they can match learners' experience and language competence. For instance, writing an email to a friend back home is more likely to strike a chord than writing about the differences between their country of origin and Australia.  Also, filling a job application form, preparing a CV, and writing a cover letter are more likely to be perceived as necessary skills than writing generally about learners' dream profession.  Thus, the instructions that precede the writing task need to be comprehensive enough to cover the linguistic, message, sociolinguistic, and cognitive aspects of writing.

Be a 'smart' teacher: Focus on your wellbeing
column16: This PD activity addressed teacher wellbeing both during the coronavirus pandemic and beyond and connects it to learner wellbeing and good teaching. The presenter, Sarah Mercer, used the acronym SMART (which stands for Self, Motivation, Activity, Relationships, and Time) to talk about building teacher confidence in teaching online English language classes to non-native speakers.   Mercer raised the valid point that while learner wellbeing is a well-known term, the concept of teacher wellbeing has become equally important of late. The push to move to online platforms in order to continue teaching students while abiding by social distancing laws in Australia as well as across the globe has often meant an increase in anxiety. This is because teaching has traditionally been a face-to-face activity and most classroom teachers have had to dive into the online world of Zoom, Google Classroom, etc with almost little to no training.
column17: One important point Sarah Mercer raised was to do with encouraging English language teachers to start teaching online from what they know to be their strengths. Once some degree of confidence is built using online platforms, English language teachers can then proceed to expand; in other words, building on one's strengths will give a positive boost to the teaching. Mercer refers to this as "self-efficacy", that is, a "yes, I can" attitude. She urges teachers to be kind to themselves in their self-evaluation and to be more realistic with workload expectations and less rigid with notions of perfection.  Another equally vital point was Mercer's linking of mental wellbeing to the physical. This can be achieved by gardening, exercising, nutrition, adequate sleeping hour, etc.  Other interesting wellbeing techniques include reminding oneself of the bigger picture; "savouring", which requires attending to positive experiences from the past, present, and future, etc.
column18: I intend to use this PD in my own teaching in the area of lesson planning and time management. Working from home has freed up time spent traveling back and forth to work among other things. As a result, I now have more time to invest in lesson planning. Although this may seemingly be a "good" thing, it is also deceptive when it leads to what Mercer calls "blurry boundaries". This is when the so-called work/life balance and division collide into each other. I have like to confine my work hours to the time I used to actually spend at work before the pandemic.
column19: A few suggestions Sarah Mercer made to proactively contend with the "spillover-crossover model" were the concepts of time-boxing and Pomodoro technique. These techniques require one to limit tasks to fixed but realistic timelines. They will assist me to set objectives and get work done within short bursts of high-intensity activities while minimising interruptions and distractions.

column16: This PD focused on a framework that would result in engaging learners with the move from face-to-face synchronous teaching to online classes with the coronavirus pandemic and subsequent lockdown in Australia. The PD trainer, Robert Martinez, maintains that the basic principles of face-to-face teaching apply to online learning. He notes that it is paramount to be more empathetic and use more gestures and intonations to minimise the physical distancing that comes with online learning. Additionally, there should be a push towards even more speaking in the online classes with writing becoming a close second in the learning objectives. Again, this would depend on the duration of the class.  The lesson framework Martinez outlined included the stages of setting the agenda where students will be informed of what they are going to learn during that particular lesson; warm-up activities that activates learners' prior knowledge; production and practice; breaks for long classes followed by more production and practice; teacher's feedback on the production; a summary at the end of the session outlining what has been taught that particular day; assigning homework; and a closing activity.
column17: Robert Martinez pointed out the importance of using the gallery view in the online platform that teachers elect to use. Asking and expecting students to also keep their webcams on during the lesson would also aid in learner engagement.   Also, articulating more is essential with lower level classes. This reminder especially applies to me as I teach Starter and Elementary classes at the moment. Also, keeping the trainer's video on the entire duration of the lesson is necessary as this would establish a sense of being connected.  Other points Martinez raised include asking ICQs (instruction checking questions) or other features like the "raise hand" feature in Zoom to ensure that learners are on the same page; using Zoom virtual backgrounds to set the theme of the lesson and, thereafter, to get students to guess what the lesson with focus on; using Jamboard and Google Docs for collaborative activities.  Finally, Martinez stated that each lesson, whether face-to-face or online, should be designed to meet at least two of the 4 Cs of education - the four Cs being collaboration, communication, creativity, and critical thinking.
column18: While I have been using the Zoom chat box to practice writing sentences with my students, I am aware this has the drawback of sometimes causing students to copy each others' answers instead of constructing their own. column17: Students expect the instructor to have 24/7 presence and every student who submits something expects teacher acknowledgement so plan accordingly. column16: To gain associated material and learn how to use Socratic Circles,  have a clear idea of how the activities work & how activities target English language and academic skills.
column17: Socratic Circles creates an environment where learners explore ideas and are willing to be ‘wrong’ through exploratory talk (Barnes, 2008). This dynamic activity engages and motivates learners to improve skills to deeply understand texts. The structured peer feedback fosters engagement and develops key skills; listening, giving opinions about ideas and responding to others. A better understanding of expectations at university level is gained, practice in debating and questioning, and awareness of weaknesses.  The activity helps focus specific goals for peer feedback and evaluation.  Learners gain strategies to practice critical reading and thinking skills rather than being told that they are not thinking deeply enough about a text. This approach also improves their listening and engages ideas to aid learners. Findings from our research indicate that 85% of learners valued feedback and 80% wanted to try the activity again.

column16: Key principles of test writing
column17: There are a complex range of factors which affect a test's fairness, validity and reliability.  Test fairness: Select accessible texts Think about the original intended audience (this should be broad not narrow)    Test validity: Create test questions that force candidates to: Scan for key information Skim read to assess relevance Read in detail to reach a conclusion Understand paraphrase and accurately transfer information   Test reliability: Each question must: have one clear answer accurately reflect the information in the text not be guessable without reading not represent a logic puzzle  Item writing: Objective items (selected response):  T/F/NG, Y/N/NG, Multiple Choice Productive items (constructed response):  Gap-fill, e.g. complete a paraphrase   With ALL items: The language in the question should be a lower level than the passage The reading load of each question should be limited  No tricksy items   Problems with Objective Items/ Selected Response (T/F/NG and Y/N/NG)  Form problems  Overlap or double dipping Locator problems  ‘’If you see an ‘odd’ statement put NG’’ Using words from the passage // mirroring the text Language: must be precise / unambiguous / objective / avoid taboos Double keys (problems with inference and accurately reflecting the text) Double / multiple propositions Reduced options = easy & unreliable – Truisms Focusing on numbers / proportions Double Negatives  Problems with Objective Items/ Selected Response (Multiple Choice):  Conventions - Problems of Form Unclear Locator Unclear Focus Not true to text  Easily dismissed options Splitting hairs – (and overlap)  Overly complex / Negative stem   Focusing on vocabulary

column16: Teach students to express an opinion and listen to each other or respond relevantly.   teach students to communicate more authentically
column17: Non-verbal signs/ semi-verbal signs Echoing - remembering and restating keywords Clarifying - paraphrasing to check the meaning Reflecting - paraphrasing meaning and emotion to build rapport/empathy Questioning and commenting - to build on speaker's ideas and thus drive the conversation  Activities: 1. An excellent friendvs a terrible friend. Divide students into groups of 3. Round 1.  Student A shares a problem. Students B is a terrible friend. Student C is the observer. Class debrief. Ask Student A what was that like. (Elicit I didn't want to continue). Ask students C what did B do to be a terrible friend (lack of eye contact, possible playing with a mobile phone). Round 2 Student A shares a problem. Student B is an observer. Student C is an excellent friend. Class debrief. Ask As what was it like? (Elicit I wanted to continue). Ask students B what did students C do. Elicit smiling, nodding, leaning in, listening noises. Extension: to analyse a video to see how people show interest.  2. "Sorry you've lost me" Students demonstrate active listening by seeking clarification. Brainstorm or pre-teach the language: Would you mind repeating that? So what was that again? Are you with me?  Sorry, I didn't catch the last part.   Put in a real context where they experience communication. The bad phone line. Students invite them to an event and give directions on how to get there. Add some background noise while students are talking.  Solve the maths problem. In pairs. 1 reads the problem when the other does the Maths.  Draw a picture. Students sit back to back and draw the pictures their partner is describing.  Reflecting Activities Pre-teach vocabulary for emotions. Pairs A and B take turns reading sentences with emotion. The listener guesses the emotion and reflects it back.  Reflecting words: Echoing.  Students imagine that they are at a cocktail party. Students write 3 impressive facts about themselves they're like to share with the people they meet. As they mingle, the listeners must echo keywords. In debrief ask how they feel when other people echoed what they said.   Mirroring the ideas of the speaker. In pairs, A reads out the sentence and B reflects the idea. column16: I wanted to know more about WIRA as I work many of the IRU candidates I work with are aligned to this project. The World Indigenous Research Alliance (WIRA) was established in 2012 as a grass-roots movement of Indigenous scholars passionate about making a global difference for Indigenous peoples and their education. Promoting ethical research practice by, with and for Indigenous peoples, WIRA is a service-oriented endeavour designed by Indigenous scholars working in mainstream institutions to support each other and to provide culturally safe spaces to share ideas. WIRA operates under the mandate of the World Indigenous Nations Higher Educational Consortium (WINHEC) who regularly report to the General Assembly of the United Nations Indigenous Peoples Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues (UNPFII) pertaining to Indigenous Peoples and their education (United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues, 2007).

column17: - The presenters compare the "knowledge code", where in order to achieve success in a field it is what you know that matters (epistemic relations), with the "knower code", where success is influenced more by who you are (and how you relate to/interact with others) (social relations).  - Different fields/professions tend to place different emphases on knowledge vs. knowing: fields such as engineering tend to privilege epistemic relations over social relations (knowledge code is emphasised), the reverse tends to be true for fashion, while in fields such as architecture both what you know, and who you are, are privileged.  - This has implications for syllabus design. For example, regulations and policy may dictate a certain model of the ideal practitioner in a field (the knowledge code), while the industry itself may prefer a different model based more on personality and interpersonal skills (the knower code), and course designers need to try and cater to both. - It also has implications for international students coming to study at a Western educational institution, depending on their academic background. If they come from an academic culture in which the knowledge code is privileged, they may feel that in an educational setting where knower-oriented teaching practices prevail (group work, pair work, peer teaching and feedback), they are not "learning" anything. This "hidden" knower code can thus disadvantage certain students. - Course designers thus need to ask themselves what assumptions about learning are "hidden" in their courses--assumptions that end up giving some students a higher chance of success than others. - The presenters then turn to the case of academic writing, and specifically the question of what makes a good paragraph. This is a social justice question, insofar as socioeconomic, cultural and academic background determine success in academic writing. People of Western, middle-class educated backgrounds will have been exposed to a wide variety of genres and will know the reader expectations associated with them (and that success is associated with conforming to these expectations. They know these rules implicitly, and therefore are privileged in Western tertiary educational systems. - People from lower SES or non-Western backgrounds are not likely to bring a knowledge of these rules with them, and are therefore disadvantaged -- so the role of the EAP practitioner is to explicitly teach these rules. - The presenters introduce the concept of the semantic wave as a "rule of the game" that determines how a good paragraph is organised in terms of density of meaning and idea specificity. Teaching ideas for helping students grasp this concept include breaking a well-written paragraph into sentences and then placing the sentences in order along an X axis, with the position on the Y axis being determined by semantic density: a wave pattern should emerge, demonstrating a broad semantic range in the paragraph. Or various graphs representing different semantic profiles can be matched to more and less well-written paragraphs.

column16: To satisfy my curiosity about LCT, which I had never heard of until it started popping up with increasing regularity on my Twitter feed, and to learn how it can be applied in the EAP classroom.
column17: - Introduces the concepts of semantic density (how much meaning is packed into a lexical item), semantic gravity (how contextualised a lexical item is) and the semantic wave to demonstrate how an orderly movement between abstraction and specificity/simplicity in language and ideas can enhance the logic and "flow" of a text and produce better writing outcomes. - The "hamburger model" of paragraph writing is inadequate because it doesn't take semantic range into account. This is why a student's paragraph may be structurally sound (it has a topic sentence, supporting sentences and a concluding sentence--even linking devices) and yet still seem poorly constructed in terms of logic and flow.  - Poorly-constructed paragraphs have flatter semantic profiles. They may have weak semantic density from beginning to end, meaning that the language and ideas remain simplistic/personalised/highly contextualised--there is no sense of the bigger picture. Or they may have weak semantic gravity throughout: composed of meaning-dense language and decontextualised ideas that are never sufficiently explained or clarified with real-world examples. - A well-constructed paragraph uses semantically-dense language (e.g. nominalisations) to introduce the main idea, explains/elaborates on the main idea (weaker SD, stronger SG), gives a real-world example (weak SD, strong SG), considers the implications of the example (stronger SD, weaker SG), and then concludes with a reminder of the main idea (strong SD, weak SG). Hence the "wave" profile. - In the classroom, these concepts can be introduced to students by (i) applying them to lexical items and ideas, then (ii) matching sample paragraphs to different semantic profiles. (iii) Using a template based on the semantic wave, students can then write their own paragraphs.
column18: - Cambridge proficiency grading sheets distinguish between "communicative achievement" and "organisation"--the concept of the semantic wave not only ties these concepts together but would also help students understand what markers are looking for in terms of "communicative achievement." - The paragraph template will come in very handy in scaffolding our bridging students' writing.

column16: Develop active listening skills. Find some fun, practical ideas that I can use in my classroom to help my learners.
column17: Activities:  1 Dual dictation Put learners into pairs A and B. When learner A is speaking, B writes down what they are saying. When learner B is speaking, A writes down what they are saying. When they finish, they put two sides of the conversation together.  You then ask learners to perform their dialogues in front of the class.  2. Class memory quizz One learner goes in front of the class. The rest of the class asks any questions. Note the answers to the questions to help you remember. Try to have half of the group answer the questions. After half the learners have been to the front, tell the class they are going to do the quiz. Put learners in teams and ask them questions about their classmates. It is one point per correct answer. The team with the most points wins.  3. Listen for lies Divide the class into 2 teams A and B. Ask one learner at a time to come in front of the class. A learner reads aloud a text which you have chosen. The learner then reads it aloud but makes some changes. The two teams listen to a learner reads a lie.  When that happens, the two teams must stand up.  The first team to stand up gets one point. The team with most points win.  Activity 4 you should prepare three cards, one for each learner in a group – A, B and C. They have two or three minutes to prepare before the activity begins. Open the headings below to read the cards for each learner. Learner A You're going to talk for two minutes about a time when you didn't know anybody and had to try to build relationships with strangers. Your story could be a success or a failure. If you can’t think of a true story, use your imagination to invent one. Use some of the following ideas to help you plan your story. Remember: you'll need to speak for two minutes. •	Where were you? Why were you there? •	Who were the other people? •	Why didn't you know anyone? •	What did you do? Did it work? •	How did you feel? •	What did you learn? Learner B A's going to tell you a story for two minutes. You're going to try to change A's mood just by the way you listen to the story. Here's how you're going to do it: •	For the first minute, listen to A's story, but don't react in any way. Just look at A with a neutral expression on your face. •	For the second minute, gradually start to appear more interested in A's story, so that by the end of the second minute you seem to be very, very interested. Learner C Your job is simply to watch A and B as they take part in an experiment. You have to work out what the experiment is, and how effective it is. Be ready to report back to them on what you observed.  Concluding the activity After the two minutes have finished, ask C in each group to tell their partners what they think the experiment was. B will then be able to confirm if they're right or not. Once again, this activity is about raising awareness of the importance of active listening. You can get feedback from each group on how B showed more interest.

column9: A theory-practice divide: EFL teachers’ and students’ beliefs about grammar instruction
column16: This journal article relates to what I see as a common issue in language schools. Teachers have routinised beliefs about what works in their classrooms in regard to teaching grammar, and these beliefs often do not reflect contemporary understandings of how we can effectively facilitate SLA. Students also possess interesting beliefs about how they learn best, also having been routinely exposed to similar methodologies over a study period, or even a lifetime in the case of adult learners. The article draws on discrepancies between teacher and student beliefs to highlight cases in which practice could better reflect theory and enable teachers to critically reflect on their methodology. The PD goal for this activity is therefore to reflect on these discrepancies in my own practice and classroom context.
column17: Key reflections:  Student attitudes towards grammar as the most important element of language learning are consistent with direct student feedback in my classroom, even to the extent that students request that more time be devoted to teacher-led grammar explanations in class. This in contrast to the typical CLT-style or CELTA-style approaches most teachers learn and routinely internalise. It strikes me that I should perhaps begin to think about teacher talk time on a per-week or even a per-course basis, rather than simply minimising it each class.  Again in regard to grammar instruction, my own beliefs about this reflect an understanding that explicit instruction should follow from authentic examples, and that these should drive learning. Yet in the study, only 48% of students preferred this approach. This raises a question - Do students really believe that rule-based, teacher-centred learning is better, or have they simply internalised this method as the only one? The responsibility for creating a more varied approach to learning lies with teachers.   Key Conclusions:  There is a need to promote a critical interaction between teachers' experiential and formal knowledge so that they can restructure their implementation accordingly. This would enable teachers to critically examine and challenge their beliefs to accommodate innovations in language teaching and in turn theorise rather than routinise their practice. PD and teacher education programs have the role of mediating that interaction - A change in teachers' beliefs will in turn lead to a change in their students' beliefs about language acquisition. All in all, it is clear that neither teacher nor student beliefs about what works well in language acquisition reflect contemporary theory and practice. It us up to teachers to engage with contemporary research and turn the classroom into a more critical space where all parties can interrogate accepted practices.
column18: Classroom goals:  1. Encourage students to attempt new methods of learning, and providing in-class time for students to be more autonomous in studying grammar. This might take the form of self-directed learning or out-of-class group assignments.  2. Prompt students (and colleagues) to think more broadly about which methods "work" and which don't, and including this in any needs analysis.  3. Question commonly held assumptions about learning styles and their perceived connections to students' cultures and home countries.
column19: 1. Require students to use out-of-class study guides and grammar references to develop their understanding independently prior to grammar lessons. Hold needs analysis sessions early in the course in which students can have meaningful input on curriculum implementation, and help them to realise that there is more than one way of studying grammar. column16: Managing class time; "flipped classrooms"; reflections on the purported efficacy of assigning homework
column17: The article, though earnest and well researched, was riddled with grammatical errors that hinted at the meta-structural insolvency that Mr. Rogers unintentionally exuded.   For example, studies he cited repeatedly relied on students' own assessments of their amount of time doing homework, without appreciating how relative that self-reflection could be. He used the fact that those who reported doing the most homework failed to score higher than those who did less as proof of the relative inefficacy of homework. The issue at hand is far more complex and his treatment of it was grossly over-simplistic; the highest scorers will naturally need less review time, since talent varies widely and isn't directly related to time spent honing a skill, and those who spend more time doing homework are clearly those least focused and/or those who struggled the most with it, unsurprisingly thus scoring lower on their exams.  In another example, he cited Bloom's taxonomy, suggesting that flipping classrooms allows for more higher-order skills to be refined during class with those of the lower-order being completed outside of class. However, the fact that this can be completely consistent with a reasonable model of homework seemed entirely lost; if ideas are presented in class and simple comprehension and application are practiced outside of class, then students can return to class and analyze, synthesize, and evaluate the ideas. "Homework" fits perfectly well into Bloom's taxonomy, and students can use that time to see if they actually understand the basics. Then class time can be used to refine that knowledge.  The question, of course, is on the quality, substance, and aim of that homework. Such a discussion should have been central to any analysis of homework, alongside a robust analysis of why many northern European test-takers score as well as their Chinese peers who spend considerably more time doing homework. This is what I had hoped for when engaging the article!

Having immense student sample sizes can mitigate variations based on individual aptitudes, and having immense instructor sample sizes can mitigate variations based on instructor effectiveness. One must rely on informed intuition, it seems, in most cases. As such, I will continue to seek ways to incorporate the facilitation of out-of-class rote learning with in-class higher order skills, trusting that I will be serving my students better as time goes on.

column17: Main challenges in managing mixed-ability classes Maintaining motivation: how to keep all students in the class motivated, interested and feeling like they are continuing to achieve. Pitch: where to ‘aim’ your lesson so that lower level students don’t fall behind, and higher level students remain challenged. Pace: managing the speed and pace of the lesson in such a way that higher level students don’t get bored and lower level students don’t feel rushed  (relates to the two points above) Managing dominant students: students with strong speaking skills can easily dominate or disrupt a class – this may also be exacerbated if they also have low reading and writing skills, and don’t want to lose face. Differentiated instruction: tailoring teaching to suit students with different educational backgrounds – for instance, general literacy and numeracy, academic literacy, grammatical background knowledge, etc. Differentiated feedback: tailoring and focusing feedback to suit the individual’s level/ability, knowing when to praise and when/how far to push.
column18: Strong + weak student pairing. Be careful to: ensure no one is losing face; ensure stronger students feel they are learning enough and not just supporting ‘weaker’ students; mix this up with other ways of pairing/grouping (see below). Vary the grouping. i.e., high/high, low/low, high/low, depending on the task. Be careful to: give strong students the opportunity to work together sometimes. Use students with higher ability in a skill as models, assistants, or even teachers (e.g., they can teach some of the target vocab). Be careful to:  make sure everyone gets a chance to shine (see below). Make sure everyone gets a chance to shine. Even weak students, if they have been monitored and supported during the task, can ‘shine’ in feedback by sharing the correct answer with the class. ‘Everyone can be the “expert” depending on the focus/skill,’ says @andrea_rivett. Use a range of graded or extension tasks. For example, jigsaws readings/listenings with more challenging or detailed tasks for stronger students, or with extra extension tasks for those who finish early. Be careful to: think about how feedback would work with different tasks (it may be easier to conduct feedback in groups rather than with the whole class). column16: I've often noticed that although some students are determined to undertake tertiary studies in Australia, the journey from being an ESL student to becoming a university one is rather bumpy and demotivating as some students feel overwhelmed with the amount of language they have to pick up on and all the progress they have to make in order to start their academic life. I feel I have to improve my teaching by finding ways to motivate them to get through the preparatory stage, that is, making them see that every time they make progress, even if that means little progress, it is still a reason to celebrate and that should be one more reason for them to work even harder towards their final goal.
column17: I believe the main take-away from this webinar is that teachers may take students' lack of motivation as disinterest uniquely. In fact, there are many factors that contribute to the 'demotivation' factor, some stemming from language barriers students do not seem to easily overcome. We (teachers) are often too quick to see it as lack of concern or curiosity, but the problem is actually much deeper and much more entrenched in the students than simply lethargy.
